podcast.title: Life-Altering Car Crash and Continued Career
podcast.body: On August 16, 2014, Mary Clayton was involved in a severe car crash in Los Angeles, which resulted in her losing both her legs, amputated below the knees. Despite these profound injuries, she has continued her career, recording both as a solo artist and as a backup singer, showcasing remarkable resilience. "Her injuries were so bad that she lost both her legs. They were amputated below the knees. But she continues to record, both as a solo artist and as a backup singer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: One of the Greatest Backup Singers
podcast.body: Mary Clayton is recognized as "one of the greatest backup singers in American music history." Her contributions to iconic songs have cemented her legacy in music. "she's one of the greatest backup singers in American music history."

srcs.episode: Ep. 3 - Nostalgia, Race, and Rebels in 70s Southern Rock (Encore)

podcast.title: Refusal and Reclaiming "Sweet Home Alabama"
podcast.body: When asked to sing backup on "Sweet Home Alabama," Mary Clayton initially refused due to the painful associations Alabama held for her as an African American woman, recalling the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing in Birmingham in 1963, Bull Connor, and George Wallace's "segregation today, segregation tomorrow, segregation forever" inaugural address in January 1963. Despite these profound reservations, her husband urged her to participate, leading her to contribute to the song as a means to claim her own experience and truth as a Black woman in the South. "She did it to claim her own experience as a black woman in the South We got your sweet home Alabama right here is her exact quote."

podcast.title: Role in "Twenty Feet From Stardom"
podcast.body: Mary Clayton's story, including her famous recording session for "Gimme Shelter," is featured in the documentary "Twenty Feet From Stardom." "She tells this story in the documentary twenty feet from stardom which you must see if you have not go find it streaming somewhere twenty feet from stardom."

podcast.title: Session Vocalist for Major Artists
podcast.body: Mary Clayton has appeared on plenty of other legendary recordings as a session vocalist, lending her voice to tracks by artists such as Leonard Skynyrd ("Sweet Home Alabama"), Joe Cocker ("Feeling All Right"), Tori Amos, Coldplay, and Ringo Starr. Her extensive work demonstrates her reputation as a highly sought-after backup singer across various genres. "Mary has also appeared on plenty of other legendary recordings, Sweet Home Alabama by Leonard Skinnerd, Feeling All Right by Joe Cocker. Tori Amos, Coldplay, Ringo Star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Acid Queen in "The Who's Tommy"
podcast.body: Mary Clayton also ventured into musical theater, appearing on the London stage in the role of the Acid Queen in a production of The Who's "Tommy." This showcases her diverse talents beyond her prolific recording career, demonstrating her versatility as a performer. "Mary has also appeared on the London stage in the role of the acid queen in a production of The Who's Tommy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tragic Miscarriage After "Gimme Shelter" Recording
podcast.body: The day after her strenuous, late-night recording session for "Gimme Shelter," Mary Clayton suffered a miscarriage, losing her little girl. She believed the physical strain and late hour of the performance contributed to this tragic event, leading her to be unable to listen to the song for many years. "The next day, Mary miscarried. She and her husband lost a little girl, and Mary thinks it might have happened because of the lightness of the hour, and the strain she put on her body with that performance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
